unit.title: Life at the Courts
unit.summary: Open play, paddle stacking, calling lines, etiquette, ratings, DUPR, de-escalation, injuries.

lessons.title: Open play and the paddle stack
lessons.objective: Know how you get on a court.

payload.prompt: At a winners-stay court, what happens when you win a game?

options.text: You stay on the court; losers go to the back of the paddle stack.
Everyone sits out for the next game.
You have to leave immediately.
The score resets and you play again.

explanation.correct: Winners stay and play the next group from the stack. Losers go to the back of the line. Some courts do it differently, so it is fine to ask how yours works.
explanation.incorrect: At a winners-stay court the winning team keeps playing and the losing team queues up again. Nobody is forced off, and the score does not reset.
explanation.sayThisLine: At a winners-stay court, winners stay and losers rotate.

payload.prompt: Put joining open play in order, from arriving to the next game.

items.text: Put your paddle in the stack with the others waiting
items.why: The stack shows whose turn is next.

items.text: Watch the current game and wait your turn
items.why: You are waiting for your paddle to come up.

items.text: Step on when your group is called
items.why: Your group is now up against the current winners.
The game has to finish before anyone rotates.

items.text: Winners stay on, and losers go to the back of the stack
items.why: That is the rotation at a winners-stay court, and it starts the cycle again.

explanation.correct: Stack your paddle, wait, step on when called, play the game, then rotate: winners stay and losers go to the back of the line.
explanation.incorrect: The order is stack, wait, play, then rotate. You only find out who stays or goes after the game is finished.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stack, wait, play, then rotate.

payload.prompt: Match each open-play term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Informal drop-in games that anyone can join, with a queue for who plays next.
Paddles lined up to show who is waiting to play, so everyone gets a fair turn.
A common rotation rule that keeps the winning team on the court for the next game.

distractorDefinitions: A way to store equipment between games

explanation.summary: Open play is drop-in and casual. You put your paddle in the stack to queue, and many courts rotate by winners-stay.
explanation.sayThisLine: Open play means a stack and a rotation. Ask how your court does it.

payload.prompt: Complete the open-play flow.
payload.template: In open play, you {{how-join}}, and after you play, {{what-happens}} if you win.

options: you stay on and play again
gaps.correct: you stay on and play again

explanation.correct: Open play: stack to join, win to stay, lose to queue again.
explanation.incorrect: The rotation is simple: paddle stack to join, winners stay, losers go to the back.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stack to play. Win to stay. Lose to wait.

payload.prompt: At a winners-stay court you just won. Do you stay on?

scene.alt: Open play scenario: the winning team is on the court at a winners-stay court.

explanation.correct: Yes. At a winners-stay court the winners play the next group from the stack, and the losers go to the back of the line.
explanation.incorrect: Winners-stay means exactly that. If your court rotates everyone off, that is a different setup, and it is worth asking about.
explanation.sayThisLine: Win and I stay. Lose and I wait.

lessons.title: Call your own lines
lessons.objective: Handle line calls fairly, incl. prompt out calls.

payload.prompt: The ball looks like it's half on, half off the line. You're calling it on your side. Do you call it out or in?

situation.narrative: A close ball lands right on the boundary line and you can't tell if it's in or out.

facts.label: Doubt rule
facts.value: Benefit of the doubt goes to the opponent

options.label: Call it in (benefit of the doubt)
options.consequence: Right. When you are not sure, the doubt goes to the other side. A ball touching the line is in anyway, and giving it keeps the game friendly.
considerations: Lines are in if any part touches
When in doubt, it is in
Fair play beats winning on a shaky call

options.label: Call it out to be safe
options.consequence: You would take a point you are not sure you earned, and that costs trust. Benefit of the doubt means close balls go to the other side.
considerations: Benefit of the doubt is the standard expectation
Questionable calls sour open play
Integrity matters more than one point

payload.expertNote: In self-officiated play, when in doubt, call it in. It keeps the game fair and fun.

payload.prompt: A ball lands out. You wait five seconds, then call it out. Fair?

scene.alt: A ball landed out of bounds, and the line call is made several seconds late.

choices.label: No, out calls must be prompt

explanation.correct: No. The current rulebook asks for out calls to be made promptly, right when you see the ball land, not after a pause to think it over.
explanation.incorrect: A call that comes seconds later, after the rally has moved on, is not prompt. The point of the rule is that everyone knows right away.
explanation.sayThisLine: If it's out, I say so right away.

payload.prompt: Match each line-call concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: In self-officiated play, each player calls the lines on their side of the court.
When unsure if a ball is in or out, call it in (give the point to the opponent).
An out call has to be made right away, not after a delay.

explanation.summary: Line calls are player-run in open play. Benefit of the doubt means when it's close, call it in. Prompt means call it right away.
explanation.sayThisLine: Call fairly: in when in doubt, out only when sure, and right away.

payload.prompt: Complete the line-call rule.
payload.template: When you're unsure if a ball is in or out, {{decision}}, because {{why}}.

options: the doubt goes to your opponents
gaps.correct: the doubt goes to your opponents

explanation.correct: Benefit of the doubt: when you are not sure, the ball is in, because the doubt goes to your opponents.
explanation.incorrect: It is about fairness, not speed. When in doubt, give your opponents the ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: If I'm not sure, it's in. The doubt goes to them.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: A ball was really close. I wasn't sure, so I called it out anyway.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Tricky one! I've learned that when you're not sure, it's in. Did they say anything?
Good call, always trust your read.
You should have called it out louder.
Silence means you were wrong.

payload.translation: Sam was unsure and still called the ball out. The usual etiquette is the other way round: if you are not sure, the ball is in, because the doubt goes to your opponents.

followUps.line: I think the etiquette is that if you're not sure, it's in. Want to offer them the point?
followUps.why: Shares what you know as something you learned, and suggests a friendly fix.

followUps.line: Those close ones are hard. Next time you're unsure, calling it in keeps everyone happy.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Sam did not mean any harm. Stay gentle: you are sharing what you just learned, not judging the call.

lessons.title: Court etiquette
lessons.objective: Know "ball on court", warm-ups, gracious wins.

payload.prompt: A loose ball from the court next to you rolls onto your court during a rally. What should someone call?

situation.narrative: Mid-rally, a stray ball from another game enters your court.

options.label: Call "Ball on court!" to stop play and alert everyone
options.consequence: Right. The call tells everyone to stop and look for the stray ball, and the rally is usually replayed once the ball is cleared.
considerations: It is a safety call
Everyone needs to know right away
The point is usually replayed

options.label: Keep playing and ignore it
options.consequence: Risk: someone could trip or step on the loose ball mid-point.
considerations: Safety is the priority
A clear call helps everyone
Stopping play is the right call

payload.expertNote: "Ball on court!" is a safety call and the right thing to do. It stops play and keeps everyone safe.

payload.prompt: What is good court etiquette in pickleball?

options.text: Warm up with your opponents, say a friendly word after the game, and leave the court tidy.
Playing as hard as you can and not wasting time.
Leaving immediately after you win.
Telling opponents when they make mistakes.

explanation.correct: Good etiquette is mostly kindness: hit a few warm-up balls with your opponents, say 'good game' at the end, and leave the court as you found it.
explanation.incorrect: Etiquette is about how you treat people. Telling opponents about their mistakes, or vanishing the moment you win, is not friendly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Warm up together, say good game, leave the court tidy.

payload.prompt: Match each etiquette practice to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A safety call to stop play when a stray ball from another court enters the playing area.
Taking time before the game starts to let both sides hit and get comfortable.
The unwritten habits of being a good court neighbor, like kind words and a tidy court.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty written into the official rulebook
A fee you pay to use the court

explanation.summary: Etiquette is mostly kindness: warm-ups, friendly words, a tidy court, and a call of 'Ball on court!' when a stray ball rolls in.
explanation.sayThisLine: Warm up together, be kind, and call 'Ball on court!' for safety.

payload.prompt: Complete the etiquette rule.

explanation.correct: Etiquette is how you treat others: respect, generosity, and care for the space.
explanation.incorrect: Good court etiquette means being kind to opponents, warming up together, and taking care of the courts.
explanation.sayThisLine: Respect, warmth, and care: that's court etiquette.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We beat them pretty badly. I just want to shake hands and move on.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Nice win! A quick 'good game' and a paddle tap is a lovely way to end it.
Doesn't matter, you won.
Tell them what they did wrong.
Leave quickly so they don't feel bad.

payload.translation: A lopsided win is a good moment to be gracious. A friendly word and a handshake or paddle tap costs nothing and keeps the court friendly.

followUps.line: Congrats! Want to tell them good game on the way off?
followUps.why: Celebrates Sam and nudges toward a friendly finish.

followUps.line: A kind word after a big win goes a long way, and they might be glad to play again.
followUps.why: Shows the practical side of being kind.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Sam already knows to be kind, so just be happy for the win. No lecture needed.

payload.prompt: Match each pickleball skill level to what it represents.

pairs.definition: Knows the rules and is working on keeping the ball in play.
More consistent, with third-shot drops and dinks starting to come together.
Steady soft game, good court awareness and good teamwork with a partner.

distractorDefinitions: Just picked up a paddle for the first time
Plays for prize money on the pro tour

explanation.summary: Ratings are rough guides to ability, and they differ a little between rating systems and clubs. Each step up usually means more consistency.
explanation.sayThisLine: 3.5 means the basics are steady and I'm building consistency.

payload.prompt: What might a 3.5 player be working on?

options.text: Consistency on the third-shot drop and patience in dink rallies.
Just learning the basic rules.
Turning pro next month.
Hitting anything other than dinks.

explanation.correct: A 3.5 usually has the basics down and is building consistency on shots like the drop, plus patience in the soft game.
explanation.incorrect: A 3.5 already knows the rules and plays real rallies. Ratings are rough guides, so two 3.5s can still look different.
explanation.sayThisLine: 3.5 means I know the game and I'm building consistency.

payload.prompt: A friend says they're a 4.0. Does that make them a pro?

choices.label: No, that's a strong club player

explanation.correct: No. A 4.0 is a strong recreational player. Touring pros are rated far higher, well past 5.0 on most scales.
explanation.incorrect: Ratings like 3.5 and 4.0 describe recreational and amateur play. Pros sit far above them, so a 4.0 is impressive but not a pro.
explanation.sayThisLine: A 4.0 is a strong club player, not a touring pro.

payload.prompt: Complete the skill-level statement.
payload.template: A higher rating usually means more {{quality}}, and it describes your {{what}}, not who you are.

explanation.correct: A rating is a rough guide to how consistent your play is right now. It can change as you play more, and it says nothing about you as a person.
explanation.incorrect: Gear and personality do not move a rating. It reflects how steady your play is today, and it changes as you improve.
explanation.sayThisLine: A rating is a snapshot of my play, not of me.

payload.prompt: You're a 3.5 and someone asks if you want to play with 4.0s. What's a good reason to say yes?

situation.narrative: You're invited to play with stronger players.

facts.label: Difference
facts.value: You may lose more, and see better play

options.label: Yes, if they're happy to have you
options.consequence: Good plan. Playing with stronger players shows you faster shots and smarter choices. Keep it light, and expect to lose a few.
considerations: Stronger players can raise your game
You see new shots up close
Check that the group is happy to mix

options.label: No, stay with 3.5s where you can win
options.consequence: Perfectly fine, especially if you want close, relaxed games. You may improve a little slower, so mixing in some games with stronger players can help.
considerations: Close games are fun too
Growth often comes from a challenge
You can mix and match

payload.expertNote: Playing up can help you improve, but there is no rush. Enjoying the game matters more than climbing a number.

payload.prompt: What is DUPR?

options.text: Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating; a system that rates players based on match results.
A league run by the PPA Tour.
The official rule book.
A paddle brand.

explanation.correct: DUPR is a dynamic rating system; your rating changes based on who you play and whether you win or lose.
explanation.incorrect: DUPR stands for Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating. It's a ranking system, not a league or equipment.
explanation.sayThisLine: DUPR: matches matter, not just self-rating.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: This guy said he was a 3.5 but he played like a 4.0. I think he sandbagged.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Sandbagging means rating yourself below your real level. Hard to know from one game, though.
Definitely. He's a cheater.
Everyone does that, no big deal.
You should have won anyway.

payload.translation: Sandbagging means deliberately playing or signing up below your true skill level to gain an advantage. One strong game does not prove it, because people also have great days and their ratings lag behind.

followUps.line: That's what sandbagging is, but one game doesn't prove it. Did he play like that all night?
followUps.why: Explains the word and stays fair to the other player.

followUps.line: Honest ratings keep tournaments fair for everyone, so it's a fair thing to care about.
followUps.why: Frames it as a shared concern without accusing anyone.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You are decoding a term, not passing judgment. Sam's suspicion might be right or wrong, so stay curious instead of accusing.

payload.prompt: Does DUPR help prevent sandbagging?

explanation.correct: Yes, it helps. A DUPR rating comes from real match results rather than self-reporting, so it is harder to hold a rating that is far too low.
explanation.incorrect: DUPR is not foolproof, but because it follows match results, a player who keeps winning easily will see the rating climb.
explanation.sayThisLine: DUPR follows match results, so a fake low rating is hard to keep.

payload.prompt: Complete the sandbagging definition.
payload.template: Sandbagging is rating yourself {{rating}} your actual skill to {{why}} in a tournament.

explanation.correct: Sandbagging is deliberately entering below your real level to play an easier bracket and win.
explanation.incorrect: Rating yourself higher is the opposite. A sandbagger plays above the level they signed up at, to gain an edge.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sandbagging is signing up below your real level to win.

payload.prompt: A friend says enter the 3.5 bracket because you'd win easily. Do you?

situation.narrative: You are signing up for a tournament. You play around a 4.0 level, but your friend says entering the 3.5 bracket would make it easy to win.

options.label: Enter the bracket that matches how you play
options.consequence: Good call. Honest entries keep brackets fair, and you will get closer matches and learn more.
considerations: Fair competition for everyone
Closer matches are more fun
Your real level tends to show anyway

options.label: Enter 3.5 to win the easy way
options.consequence: That is sandbagging. You might win, but it is unfair to players who really are 3.5s, and people notice.
considerations: It is widely seen as unsporting
Real 3.5s lose their chance at a fair bracket
Reputations travel quickly at local courts

payload.expertNote: It feels good to win, but it feels better to win fairly. Enter where your real level puts you.

payload.prompt: Put a single-elimination bracket in order, from sign-up to champion.

items.text: Teams are placed in the bracket
items.why: Before anything is played, the bracket sets who meets whom.

items.text: Winners advance and losers are out
items.why: That is what single elimination means: one loss and you are done.

items.text: The last two teams play the final
items.why: The winner of the final is the champion.

explanation.correct: Teams are placed in a bracket, round one is played, winners advance and losers are out, and the last two teams meet in the final.
explanation.incorrect: The bracket comes first, then the rounds, with each loss ending a team's run, and the final comes last.
explanation.sayThisLine: Bracket, rounds, winners advance, final.

payload.prompt: Why do tournaments use divisions by skill level?

options.text: To organize players so 3.5s play 3.5s, 4.0s play 4.0s, etc., for fair competition.
To make it easier for the organizer.
To prevent everyone from playing each other.
To charge more money.

explanation.correct: Divisions by level make tournaments fair. Everyone competes against similar-skill players.
explanation.incorrect: Divisions organize players by rating so matches are competitive and fair.
explanation.sayThisLine: Divisions by level: fair brackets for all.

payload.prompt: Match each tournament format or concept to its definition.

pairs.definition: Every team plays every other team in the group, and the most wins takes first place.
An ongoing ranking where players move up by beating someone above them.
A bracket organized by skill level (3.0, 3.5, 4.0) to create fair competition.

explanation.summary: Formats organize play: round robin is fair, ladder is ongoing, tournaments use divisions by level.
explanation.sayThisLine: Round robin, ladder, or division: each keeps play fair.

payload.prompt: In a round-robin format, does losing once mean you're out?

choices.label: No, you keep playing all your matches
Yes, one loss and you're done

explanation.correct: No. In a round robin you play every other team in your group no matter how you do, and the team with the most wins comes out on top.
explanation.incorrect: Round robin means you play all your scheduled matches, so one loss does not eliminate you. Elimination is what a bracket does.
explanation.sayThisLine: In a round robin, one loss doesn't knock you out.

payload.prompt: Complete the tournament format statement.
payload.template: In a {{format}}, every team plays {{group}}, and divisions sort players by {{how}}.

explanation.correct: A round robin has every team play every other team in the group. Divisions sort players by skill level so matches are close.
explanation.incorrect: Only winners keep playing in an elimination bracket, which is a different format. Divisions are about skill level, not names or dates.
explanation.sayThisLine: Round robin means everyone plays everyone, and divisions sort by level.

lessons.title: Bodies, shoes, common sense
lessons.objective: Know common injuries and prevention at a very general level.

payload.prompt: Your elbow is sore after two hours of open play. Should you keep playing or take a break?

situation.narrative: Pain is telling you something might be wrong.

facts.label: Possible cause
facts.value: Overuse, no warm-up, or a new paddle

options.label: Take a break and rest; see a professional if it lingers
options.consequence: Good call. Pain is a signal. Rest it, and if it does not settle, check in with a doctor or physiotherapist.
considerations: Pain is a warning
Rest stops small problems growing
A doctor or physio can tell you what it is

options.label: Play through the pain; it's probably nothing
options.consequence: Playing through soreness can turn a small issue into an injury. Conservative is better.
considerations: Overuse injuries need rest
Ignoring pain often makes it worse
Prevention is easier than recovery

payload.expertNote: If something hurts and keeps hurting, take a break and get it checked. This is general advice, not medical advice for your elbow.

payload.prompt: What helps prevent common pickleball injuries?

options.text: Wear court shoes, warm up before play, take breaks, and stop if pain persists.
Nothing matters; just play.
Stretch after but never before.
Play through pain to build toughness.

explanation.correct: Court shoes, a warm-up, regular breaks and listening to your body all help. None is a guarantee, but together they lower the odds.
explanation.incorrect: Skipping everything and pushing through pain is how small aches become injuries. A little preparation and knowing when to stop goes a long way.
explanation.sayThisLine: Warm up, wear court shoes, take breaks, and stop if it hurts.

payload.prompt: Should you wear court shoes for pickleball?

choices.label: Yes, court shoes are the better pick
No, any running shoe is just as good

explanation.correct: Yes. Court shoes are built for quick side-to-side moves, with more lateral support than a typical running shoe. That can help protect ankles and knees.
explanation.incorrect: Running shoes are built for moving forward in a straight line. Pickleball has lots of sudden sideways steps, which court shoes are designed for.
explanation.sayThisLine: Court shoes are made for side-to-side moves.

payload.prompt: Complete the injury-prevention advice.

options: stop and see a pro if pain lingers
gaps.correct: stop and see a pro if pain lingers

explanation.correct: A warm-up, good shoes and listening to your body are sensible habits for staying healthy on court.
explanation.incorrect: Skipping the warm-up, wearing the wrong shoes or pushing through pain all make injuries more likely.
explanation.sayThisLine: Warm up, wear court shoes, and stop if it hurts.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: My knee has been bugging me, but I played through it anyway. Now it's worse.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Oh no, I'm sorry. Maybe rest it and have someone check it out?
You should have toughed it out more.
Pickleball is just hard on your body.
Maybe you should quit pickleball.

payload.translation: Sam ignored a sore knee and it got worse. Resting early and getting it checked is the sensible move.

followUps.line: That sounds painful. I hope it settles soon. Have you been able to rest it?
followUps.why: Sympathy first, then a gentle question.

followUps.line: If it still hurts after a rest, it might be worth seeing a doctor or physio.
followUps.why: Points to a sensible next step without diagnosing.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You are not a doctor and do not need to sound like one. Care and a gentle suggestion are enough.

payload.prompt: What is different about singles pickleball compared to doubles?

options.text: One-on-one play on the full court; more running, less net teamwork.
The kitchen is bigger.
The serve is underhand in doubles but overhand in singles.
Scoring is completely different.

explanation.correct: Singles is one-on-one, full court, so you run much more and cover everything yourself.
explanation.incorrect: Singles is the same court and rules, just one player per side. More running, less support.
explanation.sayThisLine: Singles: one-on-one, way more running.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I played mixed doubles today (one guy, one woman per side) and it was totally different.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Ooh, tell me more! What felt different about it?
That's basically the same as regular doubles.
Mixed is harder because of the imbalance.
I don't see why mixed even exists.

payload.translation: Mixed doubles has one man and one woman on each team. It is its own format, and players often say it feels different from same-gender doubles.

followUps.line: I'd love to hear what felt different. Was it the pace or the teamwork?
followUps.why: Shows real curiosity and lets Sam lead.

followUps.line: It sounds like a fun way to mix things up and meet new people.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know what makes mixed different. Asking Sam to describe it is more fun than guessing.

payload.prompt: Match each format to its description.

pairs.definition: Two vs two; the standard format with teamwork, positioning, and partner communication.
One-on-one; the player covers the full court alone with more running and baseline play.
Two vs two with one man and one woman per team; changes strategy and dynamics.

explanation.summary: Doubles is standard team play. Singles is one-on-one. Mixed is co-ed doubles.
explanation.sayThisLine: Doubles (team), singles (solo), mixed (co-ed teams).

payload.prompt: Is singles pickleball played on the same court as doubles?

choices.label: Yes, the court is the same size
No, the singles court is smaller

explanation.correct: Yes. The court is the same size; you're just playing one-on-one instead of two-on-two.
explanation.incorrect: Singles uses the full court, same as doubles. The difference is the number of players, not the court.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same court, different format: singles is one-on-one.

payload.prompt: Complete the format comparison.
payload.template: Doubles is {{desc1}}, while singles is {{desc2}} on the full court.

explanation.correct: Doubles has two players on each side and singles has one, on the same full-size court. Mixed doubles is doubles with one man and one woman on each team.
explanation.incorrect: Singles is the one-on-one version. The court and net stay the same, but one player covers everything.
explanation.sayThisLine: Doubles is two per side, and singles is one per side.

payload.title: After a rec night mixing formats
payload.setting: You and Sam are talking after open play where they tried a few different formats.

exchanges.theirMessage: I played doubles, then singles, then mixed. My legs are toast.

replies.text: Wow, three formats in one night! I bet singles wore you out the most?
replies.theirResponse: Yes! I had to cover everything myself.
replies.coachNote: You linked singles with more running and asked about it.
Warm, but a question about the experience would keep it going.

replies.text: You should have just played doubles like normal people.
replies.theirResponse: Singles and mixed are perfectly normal.
replies.coachNote: Don't dismiss other formats as unusual.

exchanges.theirMessage: Mixed was cool because the teamwork was different. One partner was a 3.0, one was 4.5.

replies.text: That would mix up strategy. Did the skill gap make it harder or more fun?
replies.theirResponse: More fun, actually. We had to play smart, not just hard.
replies.coachNote: You asked about the experience and the skill dynamic.
Polite, but a follow-up question would show real interest.

replies.text: That seems unfair to the weaker player.
replies.theirResponse: Actually, everyone played at their level.
replies.coachNote: Mixed formats can work for all levels; don't assume imbalance means unfair.

payload.closingNote: Recreational pickleball offers many formats: doubles (standard), singles (one-on-one), and mixed (co-ed). Each has a different feel and appeal.
